routes.description: Establish theism as a legitimate personal explanation whose simplicity and divine purposes make the universe's order, consciousness, moral agency, and associated general features more probable than they would be without God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent personal-explanation framework, connects simplicity to prior probability, derives relevant expectations from the proposed divine nature, and accounts for apparent counterevidence without losing the comparative explanatory inference.

motionBridge.description: Show that a simple divine-agent hypothesis makes the universe and its general features sufficiently more expected than relevant non-theistic alternatives to count as the most probable explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish purposive personal causation as a genuine and applicable explanatory mode alongside explanation through physical states and laws.
Justify simplicity as a basis for assigning prior probability while retaining evidential fit and predictive accuracy as constraints on hypothesis choice.
Derive reasons for a perfectly good and powerful God to create an orderly, life-producing universe containing conscious agents with consequential freedom.
Reconcile grave suffering and other apparent tensions with the proposed divine nature through morally relevant opportunity, obligations toward sufferers, or compensating goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify how economy in entities, properties, and mathematical structure operates in ordinary explanatory and scientific comparisons.
Connect regular natural laws and embodied conditions to the possibility of rational consciousness, purposive action, and morally significant choice.

routes.description: Deny that the proposed divine hypothesis earns the claimed comparative probability by challenging its explanatory category, simplicity, predictive specificity, coherence, and ability to accommodate suffering and human nature.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more indispensable links from divine simplicity to explanatory probability fails, or if the hypothesis remains insufficiently discriminating, internally strained, or poorly aligned with major features it is offered to explain.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available general features do not warrant treating God as the simplest and most probable explanation because the proposed comparison lacks a justified or adequately predictive basis.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the exhaustiveness or applicability of the division between inanimate causal explanation and purposive personal explanation.
Show that competing notions of simplicity can diverge and that an infinite, qualified divine agent may not be simple in the sense relevant to probability.
Require theism to provide discriminating expectations rather than unrestricted compatibility with possible observations or merely general explanatory coverage.
Test whether the extent and distribution of severe suffering are compatible with the purposes and obligations attributed to a perfectly good and omnipotent creator.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the proposed personal cause to address its fit with established causal knowledge, evolutionary explanation, and physical accounts of space and time.
Examine whether an independently created immaterial component coheres with evolutionary development, embodied cognition, and the biological cost of the human brain.

sections.title: Personal, physical, and purposive explanation
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether divine agency belongs to a defensible explanatory category and whether the proposed contrast with physical causation is sufficiently complete to support the wider inference.

sections.title: Simplicity as a guide to explanatory probability
sections.rationale: The motion expressly links simplicity with probability, making the meaning, justification, and limits of simplicity central to the comparison between theism and alternative hypotheses.

sections.title: Predicting order, life, consciousness, and agency
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the proposed divine nature generates substantive expectations for the universe's general features and whether those expectations distinguish theism from rival accounts.

sections.title: Divine attributes, physical coherence, and human nature
sections.rationale: Questions about temporality, knowledge, unlimited power, souls, evolution, and embodiment bear on whether the explanatory hypothesis is coherent and appropriately connected to the phenomena invoked.

sections.title: Suffering, moral freedom, and posthumous compensation
sections.rationale: Severe and unevenly distributed suffering is major apparent counterevidence to a perfectly good creator, while freedom, victim benefit, and compensation supply the corresponding reconciliatory requirements.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Personal explanation through an animate agent's purposes, beliefs, and powers is a genuine explanatory mode alongside explanation by prior physical states and natural laws.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is a continuous portion of Swinburne's opening speech and uses his explicit first-person terminology and example.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the proposed category of personal explanation through purposes, beliefs, and powers; it has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly and clearly supplies a foundational explanatory category.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory category and its contrast with physical-law explanation are plainly recoverable and consistently expressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim is adequately supported by the familiar structure of intentional action used in the passage.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The agent-purpose-belief-power structure coherently distinguishes an intentional explanatory form, with only applicability to a divine agent left for later.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary intentional action provides representative support, though the move does not independently establish applicability beyond embodied agents.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable personal-causation framework at the top of the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is addressed within this initial constructive move.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly contrasts Newtonian explanation with explanation through an animate being's purposes, beliefs, and powers.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Explanatory practice favors hypotheses that posit fewer entities, properties, laws, and mathematical complications, as illustrated by ordinary and scientific comparisons among otherwise viable explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: This uninterrupted argument remains within Swinburne's opening address and develops his own stated definition and scientific examples.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines explanatory simplicity through economy in postulated entities, properties, laws, and mathematical structure, without an earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives concrete scientific content to a central simplicity principle.

precisionFindings.rationale: The economy criterion is clear, but the conditions under which competing kinds of economy govern are only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The scientific examples support a preference for economy, but do not by themselves establish a unified probabilistic rule.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from fewer postulates to explanatory preference is coherent, though the bridge among several simplicity dimensions remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scientific examples support the practice described, but rival simplicity measures and evidential-fit conditions are not yet compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central simplicity-to-probability bridge and is highly placed within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage develops its own simplicity account rather than testing a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage invokes Newtonian gravitational law as a mathematically economical hypothesis and contrasts it with indefinitely many alternatives.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: A perfectly good and omnipotent God has reason to create rational conscious beings able to make serious, consequential choices between good and evil rather than beings programmed only to do good.
moves.attributionBasis: Swinburne explicitly labels this as his hypothesis and develops the divine attributes and creative rationale in one continuous passage.

response.rationale: This constructive move derives a proposed divine reason for creating conscious agents capable of serious choices, and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly supplies a central expectation from the attributed divine goodness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The freedom rationale is recoverable, while the scope and degree of evil required for serious choice remain implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A reason for consequential freedom is supplied, but alternative ways a good creator might secure agency are not compared.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The transition from goodness to valuable unprogrammed choice is coherent, but the necessity and permissible scale of evil remain implicit bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is primarily a moral assertion about the value of choice, without developed comparison to safer forms of agency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable divine-expectations bridge by deriving consequential rational freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: No contrary account is developed sufficiently in this constructive passage to require a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly argues that God would prefer chosen good over programmed good and therefore allow serious choices between good and evil.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Theism makes an orderly, life-producing universe containing conscious embodied agents probable because regular laws enable agency and evolution, whereas physics alone does not explain why conscious beings exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The extended first-person argument occurs wholly within Swinburne's opening speech and culminates in his explicit comparative probability conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents the principal comparative prediction that theism makes orderly laws, evolution, and consciousness probable; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it reaches the motion-level comparative inference and integrates several general features.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is clear, but the relevant non-theistic alternatives and degree of probability are insufficiently delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Reasons for divine production are offered, but the strong dismissal of physical explanation and comparative probability claim outrun the supplied comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The divine-purpose account connects order to agency, but the move compresses the inference from physical incompleteness to theism's comparative probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage identifies evolution, regular laws, and consciousness, yet gives little defended likelihood comparison against non-theistic rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly advances the motion-level requirement that theism make the universe's general features comparatively probable.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move asserts its comparison without engaging a sufficiently developed rival interpretation in this passage.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links God to evolutionary laws and consciousness and asserts that physics alone cannot explain consciousness without additional categories.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Purposive behavior in evolved organisms and algorithmic systems shows that explanation is not exhaustively divided between mechanical processes and personal agents.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican has been formally introduced and explicitly identifies Richard's two explanatory kinds before presenting his objections and examples.

components.text: Whether physical-law and personal explanations exhaust the relevant kinds of purposive causal explanation.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the proposed division as non-exhaustive and states that evolved and algorithmic systems exhibit purposive behavior explainable without a personal agent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive exhaustiveness inference and supplies two counterexample classes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterexample claim is clear, although purposive behavior and purposive explanation are not kept fully distinct.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples defeat a strict dichotomy, though their bearing on irreducible personal explanation is more limited than the categorical conclusion suggests.

charity.alternative: Swinburne may recognize evolved purposive systems while retaining personal explanation as a distinct category.
charity.decisiveQualification: Recognition of intermediate systems still defeats only an exhaustive dichotomy, not the existence of personal explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Algorithmic and evolved counterexamples coherently challenge exhaustiveness, with a bounded ambiguity between purposive behavior and explanatory type.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Chess algorithms and Darwinian functions are concrete representative cases, though the deeper causal taxonomy is not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central challenge to the proposed explanatory framework.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican expressly notes that Swinburne might not object, fairly preserving the narrower force of the criticism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites algorithmic chess behavior and evolved plants and animals before concluding that explanation is not simply mechanical or personal.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Simplicity is not a unitary guide to probability because descriptive, ontological, and computational simplicity can diverge, while scientific progress sometimes favors more complex hypotheses.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican expressly attributes the emphasis on simplicity to Richard and then supplies a sustained historical and conceptual criticism.

components.text: Whether a single simplicity preference can connect fewer postulates to greater explanatory probability.

response.rationale: The reply identifies divergent descriptive, ontological, and computational criteria and notes historical movement toward more complex but better-supported theories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the central inference by showing why an unqualified unitary simplicity metric is inadequate.

precisionFindings.rationale: The several notions of simplicity and the limited conclusion that they may diverge are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples adequately establish plurality and possible divergence without claiming that simplicity is never evidentially relevant.

charity.alternative: Simplicity may operate only among hypotheses with comparable fit and may combine several economy measures.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even under that interpretation, the weighting and reconciliation of divergent simplicity measures require justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction among simplicity dimensions directly and validly undercuts an unqualified inference from simplicity to probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Conceptual distinctions and scientific-history examples provide strong support, with detailed case verification remaining compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the central simplicity-adequacy burden at the strongest end of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves a legitimate role for simplicity while identifying the unresolved choice among its different forms.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage expressly distinguishes descriptive or syntactic simplicity from ontological simplicity and invokes scientific movement toward more complex hypotheses.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Bodiless instantaneous agency is unlike observed causation, and scientific history's retreat from intuitive purposive explanations makes background fit relevant even to a cosmic hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican directly reconstructs Richard's background-knowledge position and follows it with an extended objection grounded in experience and scientific history.

components.text: Whether the proposed personal explanatory mode is applicable to an unembodied cosmic agent given established causal knowledge.

response.rationale: The reply contacts applicability by contrasting bodiless instantaneous agency with experience and by citing science's retreat from intuitive purposive accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses background fit, though it does not deny that ordinary embodied personal explanation is genuine.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clearly limited to background fit and historical applicability rather than a universal impossibility claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers background considerations against the analogy without treating historical retreat as a deductive disproof.

charity.alternative: A unique cosmic cause may reasonably lack close analogues in ordinary causal experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: Uniqueness does not by itself make background fit irrelevant to comparative probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical and experiential considerations coherently bear on prior fit, although their transfer to a unique cosmic hypothesis is not decisive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Aristotelian purposive explanations provide concrete historical support, but the broader claimed scientific trend is selectively illustrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary background-fit bridge without directly completing the central category challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly targets probabilistic fit rather than caricaturing the divine cause as logically impossible.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes science's retreat from Aristotelian purposive explanations and disputes setting aside fit with background knowledge.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: An unrestricted creator hypothesis can be verbally simple yet explanatorily non-specific, while observed natural purposiveness is explained through Darwinian evolution operating with physical mechanisms.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains in Millican's uninterrupted response and presents an explicit parody followed by his observation about natural purposiveness.

components.text: Whether a verbally simple creator hypothesis yields discriminating expectations for observed general features.
Whether verbal economy alone makes a hypothesis explanatorily preferable when it lacks specificity.

response.rationale: The reply identifies non-specificity as the failure in a simple creator explanation and contrasts it with Darwinian purposiveness operating through physical mechanisms.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both simplicity and predictive-content demands, explicitly stating the defeating consequence of non-specificity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between verbal simplicity, predictive specificity, and Darwinian mechanism is plainly and stably stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The example supports the limited conclusion that simplicity without specificity is explanatorily inadequate.

charity.alternative: The divine hypothesis includes attributes and purposes that could restrict what a creator is expected to produce.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those restrictions must still generate observations more specific than unrestricted creator intention.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The simple-but-hopeless example validly separates concise description from discriminating explanatory content.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The creator-intention example and Darwinian contrast concretely support the criticism, though no formal likelihood comparison is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central predictive-content burden by requiring specificity from the creator hypothesis.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies a legitimate strongest alternative but only briefly addresses how divine attributes might constrain predictions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt labels a simple creator-intention explanation hopelessly non-specific and points to Darwinian purposiveness combined with physical processes.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: An infinite divine agent is not straightforwardly simple because its powers have qualifications concerning evil and future free actions, and sustaining every particle implies immense computational capacity.
moves.attributionBasis: The move occurs within Millican's uninterrupted opening rebuttal turn and explicitly addresses Swinburne's account of divine infinity.

components.text: Whether an infinite divine agent is simple under the relevant economy criteria rather than merely verbally concise.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests divine simplicity through qualifications on power and knowledge and through the computational demands of sustaining every particle.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive simplicity application with several concrete complications, though their common metric is not fully defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The qualifications are concrete, but computational simplicity shifts metric relative to the preceding ontological and descriptive criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately presents the considerations as reasons the infinite agent is not straightforwardly simple.

charity.alternative: Infinite power may be specified by one simple limit-free principle despite infinitely many possible acts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Exceptions concerning evil and future free choices still require specification and may affect total complexity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The exceptions coherently complicate a limit-free specification, though computational capacity does not automatically entail complex description.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The attributed qualifications are specific, but the inference from sustaining particles to hypothesis complexity needs a defended complexity measure.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly reaches the central adequacy of divine simplicity at a high position within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism allows the appeal of a simple infinite principle while identifying qualifications that remain explanatorily relevant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies inability to do evil, lack of foreknowledge of free acts, and particle-by-particle sustenance as qualifications or burdens on simplicity.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A temporal God who knows everything up to a universal present but not future free actions appears incompatible with general relativity's denial of absolute simultaneity.
moves.attributionBasis: The challenge is delivered continuously by Millican during his rebuttal and directly names the commitments he attributes to Swinburne.

components.text: Whether the temporal and epistemic divine attributes used to accommodate free agency cohere with physical accounts of time.

response.rationale: The reply contacts coherence by contrasting a universal divine present with relativity's frame-dependent simultaneity, though it does not address the value of freedom itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly raises a physical-coherence problem for the attributed model but only indirectly bears on the target's main moral rationale.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional incompatibility between a universal present and relative simultaneity is clearly recoverable and appropriately scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument is framed as an apparent coherence problem rather than a conclusive contradiction.

charity.alternative: God's knowledge might be indexed to frames or formulated without a privileged universal present.
charity.decisiveQualification: That alternative would require revising or explaining the attributed time-T account of divine knowledge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conflict between absolute simultaneity and relativity is coherently posed, conditional on the accuracy of the attributed divine-time model.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: General relativity supplies relevant established background, though the exact theological model and possible covariant formulations are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary background-fit bridge rather than directly defeating divine reasons for agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly targets the specific temporal model while leaving room for differently formulated divine knowledge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt juxtaposes God's knowledge up to a universal time T with general relativity's relativity of simultaneity.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A freedom-based justification does not explain severe suffering and early death that deprive infants and other victims of opportunities to exercise morally significant agency.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly directs this objection to Swinburne near the end of his uninterrupted opening rebuttal turn.

components.text: Whether consequential freedom explains suffering that removes rather than enables a victim's opportunity for moral agency.

response.rationale: The reply identifies victims deprived of agency as a counterexample to the freedom rationale and states that their suffering is therefore hard to explain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive freedom premise and presents cases where the proposed good is unavailable to the sufferer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly limited to severe suffering and premature death that substantially deprive victims of agency.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move characterizes the cases as hard to explain rather than claiming deductive incompatibility.

charity.alternative: Others' agency, social responsibility, or later goods might partly explain suffering not chosen by the victim.
charity.decisiveQualification: The victim's own lost opportunity and the extreme distribution of harm still require a morally sufficient account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cases directly expose a mismatch between a freedom-enabling rationale and suffering that eliminates the sufferer's agency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Starving infants and murdered children are concrete representative counterexamples, though broader theodicies are not exhaustively compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable central counterevidence bridge through the distribution of severe suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection targets a genuine residual problem without assuming that only the victim's immediate freedom could ever matter.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage points to infants who starve and victims exterminated before gaining meaningful power to make morally significant choices.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Purposiveness in causal explanation requires a purposive agent: biological functions can be explained through selection, while ordinary goal-directed action exemplifies irreducibly personal causation.
moves.attributionBasis: The move begins with Swinburne's answer to Millican and continues within Swinburne's clearly bounded rebuttal turn.

components.text: Whether algorithmic and evolved purposiveness supplies a causal explanatory type beyond physical selection and personal agency.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes biological function explained by selection from ordinary action directed by purposes and beliefs, thereby defending the proposed causal taxonomy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses the counterexamples and explains how each is assigned within the defended categories.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction is clear, though the claim that no other causal explanatory kinds exist is broader than the examples establish.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support irreducible ordinary agency but do not exhaustively rule out every additional causal category.

charity.alternative: Purposive systems may be physically realized yet warrant higher-level explanations not reducible to personal agency.
charity.decisiveQualification: Higher-level description does not necessarily constitute a third fundamental causal explanatory mode.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The selection-versus-agent distinction coherently answers biological examples, but the exhaustive conclusion retains an underdeveloped bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Planning, promise-keeping, and selection give representative support, while algorithmic systems receive less detailed treatment.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con side's central explanatory-framework challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly accommodates evolutionary function, though it compresses the status of autonomous algorithmic explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes human plans guided by purposes and beliefs, while the wider selected passage assigns biological purposiveness to Darwinian selection.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: Among hypotheses that adequately fit the evidence, greater simplicity raises prior probability, although even a simple hypothesis must be rejected when its predictions conflict with the data.
moves.attributionBasis: Swinburne develops the point throughout his uninterrupted rebuttal turn while directly answering Millican's scientific counterexamples.

components.text: Whether scientific acceptance of more complex theories defeats simplicity as a probabilistic guide.
Whether simplicity remains relevant when explanatory fit and predictive accuracy impose additional constraints.

response.rationale: The response replaces unconditional simplicity with comparison among hypotheses adequately fitting the data and illustrates why accuracy can justify added terms, but it does not resolve divergent simplicity metrics or divine computational complexity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a justified and useful reframe of the scientific-history objection, while leaving a decisive plurality-of-metrics component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fit-qualified role for simplicity is expressly stated and consistently distinguished from predictive accuracy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately conditional on adequate evidential fit and is supported by the supplied scientific example.

charity.alternative: Millican's objection concerns divergent simplicity measures, not merely science accepting complexity for accuracy.
charity.decisiveQualification: The fit condition answers historical counterexamples but does not determine how competing simplicity measures should be weighted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional rule coherently reconciles simplicity with predictive accuracy, leaving only the choice of simplicity metric unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Boyle-Charles and van der Waals comparison concretely supports the fit qualification, though broader probabilistic justification remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con simplicity-adequacy burden by preserving a constrained role for simplicity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly handles one strong component of the objection but omits the decisive metric-plurality qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains that the more complex van der Waals law replaced a simpler law because it predicted more accurately, then limits simplicity to adequately fitting hypotheses.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Theism's generality yields too little precision to share the evidential standing of scientific hypotheses whose unfamiliarity or complexity is justified by accurate, discriminating predictions.
moves.attributionBasis: The move is delivered by Millican after the floor changes to him and explicitly follows up Swinburne's preceding account of simplicity.

components.text: Whether the fit-qualified simplicity rule gives theism sufficiently precise and discriminating predictive content.
Whether broad expectations of order and consciousness are precise enough to support comparative probability.

response.rationale: The reply accepts simplicity among equally precise hypotheses but argues that scientific complexity earns support through accurate predictions that the general theistic hypothesis lacks.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the fit qualification and the outstanding demand for discriminating predictions.

precisionFindings.rationale: Precision, specificity, scope, and simplicity are clearly separated, and the conclusion is appropriately comparative.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move grants the valid ceteris-paribus role for simplicity while limiting its force when precision differs.

charity.alternative: Theism may predict only broad general features because a free creator's particular choices are not mechanically determined.
charity.decisiveQualification: Broad compatibility still supplies weaker discrimination unless probabilities over possible divine choices are defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument validly distinguishes simplicity among equal-fit hypotheses from the need for specificity and predictive accuracy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scientific prediction supplies a concrete comparison, although the degree of theism's imprecision is not quantitatively demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central demand for discriminating predictive content.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism preserves the strongest ceteris-paribus simplicity claim while identifying the remaining predictive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes preference for the simpler of equally precise laws and contrasts this with complex theories justified by accurate predictions.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A separately created immaterial soul fits poorly with a long evolutionary history and the development of a resource-intensive human brain if the soul itself performs human thinking.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument remains in Millican's continuous turn and identifies Swinburne's soul theory before drawing its evolutionary consequences.

components.text: Whether divine production of conscious agents coheres with evolutionary embodiment and the functional cost of large brains.
Whether an independently created soul supplies a coherent mechanism for rational conscious agency.

response.rationale: The reply directly asks why long biological development and resource-intensive brains are needed if an immaterial soul independently performs the thinking.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the embodied-consciousness mechanism and identifies the missing evolutionary fit story.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clearly conditional on the attributed claim that the immaterial soul itself performs human thinking.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move requests a coherent fit account rather than claiming that evolution deductively excludes an immaterial soul.

charity.alternative: The brain may provide sensory, behavioral, or developmental capacities needed by an immaterial thinking subject.
charity.decisiveQualification: That interaction account must explain why cognitive capacity tracks the costly evolved brain so closely.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional tension between independent soul cognition and costly brain evolution is clearly and coherently derived.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolutionary duration and large-brain cost are specific relevant facts, though detailed neuroscience and interaction alternatives are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary human-nature bridge without directly completing the motion-level comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection leaves conceptual room for interaction while accurately identifying the explanatory burden that remains.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts 13.8 billion years of physical development and enormous brains with a soul inserted by divine fiat that allegedly can think by itself.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.proposition: God's omnipotence permits posthumous compensation, and God's obligation as creator requires giving sufferers an afterlife when necessary to ensure that each person's total life is good overall.
moves.attributionBasis: Swinburne advances the argument in his concluding response, with the speaker turn remaining continuous until Millican resumes.

components.text: Whether God can meet obligations toward victims whose earthly suffering or premature death deprives them of a good life.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the victim-centered demand by invoking omnipotent posthumous compensation and a creator's obligation to make each total life good overall.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers what God could owe sufferers, though it does not explain how compensation restores the particular lost agency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The obligation and total-life standard are clear, while what makes compensation adequate remains materially under-specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Omnipotence supports ability, but the asserted creator obligation and adequacy of total-life compensation need further moral warrant.

charity.alternative: Some earthly losses may be non-fungible and cannot be repaired merely by later benefits.
charity.decisiveQualification: A good total life does not automatically restore the specific opportunity for embodied moral development.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Ability plus obligation coherently yields an afterlife response, but the bridge from later good to adequate compensation remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move chiefly asserts a moral obligation and total-life criterion without defending why later goods compensate every severe loss.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con side's central moral-evidence burden by proposing obligations and compensation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses overall welfare but omits the strongest qualification concerning irretrievable developmental loss.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that omnipotence enables an afterlife and that a creator is obligated to ensure a sufferer's total life is good.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Posthumous compensation neither follows from a terrible earthly life nor restores the lost embodied opportunity of children killed prematurely to develop moral character.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican begins a new and clearly attributed turn by identifying Swinburne's immediately preceding life-after-death response as his target.

components.text: Whether later benefits can compensate for the specific lost opportunity of prematurely killed children to develop moral character.
Whether the freedom rationale applies to victims prevented from developing consequential agency.

response.rationale: The reply identifies non-restorable developmental opportunity as the defect in total-life compensation and states that later benefit does not show how those earthly lives become worthwhile.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive adequacy inference and connects it to the original freedom rationale.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly limited to specific developmental losses caused by premature death rather than all conceivable compensation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the point as a serious logical and moral difficulty, not a demonstrated impossibility of every afterlife account.

charity.alternative: Posthumous existence might include new opportunities for agency and character development.
charity.decisiveQualification: New opportunities would not literally restore the embodied childhood development and choices that were lost.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between adding later benefits and restoring an irretrievable developmental opportunity directly undermines the compensation inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Prematurely killed children furnish concrete cases, though the metaphysics of possible posthumous development is not fully examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central moral-evidence burden by challenging the adequacy of the offered compensation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply targets the non-identity of replacement benefits and lost opportunities without denying that later goods could have value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes that starving or murdered children never received the chance to develop character and questions how later life could make that loss worthwhile.
